description: A group of high school students who are interested in mathematics and physics and enjoy expanding their knowledge.
summary:
Our project is a website that transforms raw astronomical data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission into visual images of the universe. We developed a tool that allows users to enter the coordinates of a specific region of the sky (with Right Ascension (ra) and Declination (dec) coordinates) or name the object they want to see, and generate images using the available telescope data that display the chosen target in multiple wavelengths. Our website also has a 3D astronomical map that allows users to explore objects and locations, learn about them, and compare them to SPHEREX data, making it a useful educational tool.

The platform aims to make it easier to explore and compare observations taken at different times, helping users identify moving objects, changes in brightness, and other astronomical phenomena through the use of a blink comparator. By converting complex scientific data into accessible visual representations, we aim to adress the challenge of making SPHEREx’s massive dataset easier for the public to explore and understand.

This project is important because it makes astronomical exploration more accessible, encourages public participation in scientific discovery, and helps people contribute to identifying objects in the incredible amounts  of data collected by SPHEREx, as well as to understand these objects and their position in the universe.
details:
The project works by taking astronomical data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission and processing it with Python to generate images of specific regions of the sky based on coordinates (ra/dec) or the selection of a particular object. The analysis script extracts the information about the object from the IRSA archive and uses it to create 6 images from SPHEREx's six detectors, each covering a different range of infrared wavelengths, and compare the images of the object at different times using a blink comparator. It also has a 3D, explorable model of the universe where users can select and explore objects, receive data, and compare them to SPHEREx images. The website uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to display the generated images and to create a simple interface for users to interact with the data. It uses python for the analysis of the raw SPHEREx data.

The main factors we considered during development were the data processing, website usability, the way to use our processing system for images and connect it with the frontend, and the ability to handle new SPHEREx data as it becomes available. We also focused on making the process of turning raw astronomical data into images as simple and efficient as possible.

Our project aims to allow people to explore NASA SPHEREx data in a way that is simple and understandable, as well as easy to explore thanks to the 3D model. we aim to encourage the use and understanding of this satellite imagery and to promote citizen science in the identification of moving objects using the blink comparator. Our solution is new and innovative, displaying images in a single, easy to use website and connecting them with a modern 3D astronomical model. The reason this matters is that astronomical data only has scientific value when people can access, interpret and use it. By turning complex data into interactive visualizations, we aim to bridge this gap between professional research and public participation.

SPHEREx is not just any satellite. It scans the sky in 102 near infrared bands, collecting data of the entire sky. SPHEREx has multiple purposes: investigating the history of galaxy formation and matter in the universe, studying cosmic evolution, and, among others, to create a scientific resource for astronomical investigations with its all sky survey. So, by making SPHEREx data easier to explore, we want to engage with this purpose and help people interact with a very complete astronomical dataset.

Modern astronomical data is not always easy to understand. It can come in complicated formats such as .FITS files and require specialized knowledge to analyze. This creates an accessibility problem that can make people believe that these subjects are simply out of their reach unless they are experts. Our platform simplifies this process entirely. People only have to search for objects and can receive multiple observations, images, and data, compare across time, and develop an understanding of new concepts regarding wavelengths, cosmic evolution, astronomical mapping, and more. With this, we want to reduce the technical knowledge necessary to get started with astronomical research and understanding, as well as developing scientific literacy. NASA states that over 650 citizen scientists have co-authored publications and they have 49 projects open to anyone, which we believe is proof of the importance of accessibility with data.

While it may seem incredibly simple, our blink comparator is based on a real, historically important astronomical technique. Astronomers would compare multiple observations by switching them quickly and use them to determine moving objects, since they seemed to jump out against stationary backgrounds. A famous example is the discovery of Pluto in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh. This shows how a simple technique could help in an important discovery.

Infrapix is designed around allowing exploration of spatial distribution of astronomical objects and learning information about them, including general facts and spectral information. With this, it becomes a useful educational tool as well, developing visualization and reasoning in STEM education.
projectRefs: Finding Pluto With the Blink Comparator
